## Files and context

- `project/state.md`, `project/brief.md`, `project/advice.md`: r03 is the accepted aligned candidate; fine weak-pi ODMR selects 3.8759 GHz on the scan grid. Earlier Ramsey runs did not establish T2* or 13C.

## Calculations and observations

`python ramsey_check.py` compares combined raw signal, signal/reference ratio, signal divided by a linear reference fit, odd/even averages and tau > 0.2 µs. It scans 0.5–3 MHz using a linear baseline plus sine and cosine, maximizing fractional baseline-residual reduction; amplitudes are sinusoid amplitudes, not peak-to-peak. It also compares first and second halves in actual snake acquisition order. This simple half comparison is a screening check, not the project's formal drift classifier.

The old ratio screen peaks at 1.192 MHz (amplitude 0.0363, residual reduction 0.656). The new ratio peaks at 1.624 MHz (0.0255, 0.430); the predicted shifted 1.692 MHz gives 0.0250 and 0.411, while 1.192 MHz gives 0.0051 and 0.017. The empirical shift is +0.432 MHz versus +0.500 MHz programmed. This is suggestive of detuning tracking, but the 1.920 µs span gives only ~0.521 MHz nominal inverse-span resolution; grid spacing is not frequency uncertainty.

The new raw signal and reference-line-normalized signal instead have their strongest screened component at 0.882 MHz (raw amplitude 1.53 kcps, reduction 0.577); reference itself has a 0.924 MHz component (0.405 kcps, reduction 0.292), so common-mode structure and ratio sensitivity matter. The raw signal also has amplitude 1.23 kcps at 1.692 MHz (reduction 0.427). Ratio median point SEM across averages is 0.0126, signal SEM 0.711 kcps. The odd-average ratio screen peaks at 0.848 MHz, even at 1.604 MHz; excluding tau ≤ 0.2 µs moves the combined ratio maximum to 0.746 MHz. Thus the apparent tracking is not robust to data selection and readout treatment. At 1.307 and 2.076 MHz the full-ratio amplitudes are 0.0095 and 0.0062, respectively; these are single-frequency screens, not resolved sidebands.

Recorded snake order is present for all 12 averages. The first/second-half combined-readout changes range from −2.3% to +3.8%; no large monotonic loss is evident in this coarse check, but it cannot replace a formal scan-order-aware drift review. Previous run's formal review reported no drift flags.

## Interpretation and limits

A detuning-responsive Ramsey component near 1.6–1.7 MHz is plausible, but the competing ~0.9 MHz raw/reference structure, subset dependence, short time span and noise prevent a clean carrier assignment. The 0.432 MHz shift is compatible with the planned diagnostic at this limited resolution, not a precise frequency measurement or proof of a physical carrier. A transient, drift, readout normalization or multiple components could contribute.

Neither a quantitative T2* nor nearby 13C coupling or absence of coupling is supported. The earlier descriptive ~6.33 µs fit is not a measurement: the short window and uncertain signal model do not constrain decay reliably. The expected ~0.385 MHz sideband spacing is smaller than the nominal inverse-span resolution, so this dataset alone cannot resolve the proposed carrier/sideband structure.

Perform a formal scan-order-aware drift review of the completed export and inspect phase-resolved raw signal/reference and acquisition-order subsets. Then design a targeted control of pulse/readout and detuning response, preferably interleaving at least two detunings and a reference/control to distinguish common-mode or sequence artifacts; choose a longer tau window only after a reproducible carrier and adequate contrast are demonstrated. Avoid another blind repeat and defer T2*/13C fitting until the carrier and decay are supported.

Average reference levels vary from 42.0 to 55.2 kcps; no formal scan-order drift analyzer was available or run. Balanced snake direction reduces but does not eliminate drift and baseline concerns.

A 1 MHz carrier has a 1 us period, so this window spans only 1.92 cycles. The FFT bin spacing is 0.508 MHz: it cannot resolve the model's 0.615 and 1.385 MHz sidebands cleanly from 1 MHz. Frequency scans with a floating linear baseline are highly correlated at low frequency; their largest amplitude occurs at the 0.3 MHz search boundary, so it is not a reliable spectral peak. Detuning offset, pulse/timing behavior, baseline drift, and noise remain alternatives. The expected 13C Larmor scale from project context is approximately 0.384 MHz, not proof of a 13C feature.

No robust numeric T2* or bound, resolved 13C coupling or absence of 13C, or confirmed programmed-detuning-following carrier is established. `python ramsey_check.py` compares both exports. It fits a constant, linear baseline and sine/cosine on a 0.4-3 MHz frequency grid to raw signal, signal divided by a linear reference fit, and point-wise ratio, with full data and after omitting 5 or 10 initial points. It reports fixed-frequency amplitudes, per-point across-average SEM, and reference slopes in acquisition order; this exploratory scan is not a calibrated significance test. The explicit model predicts a +0.5 MHz shift of the previous 1.192 MHz feature to 1.692 MHz if it is a det-following carrier; expected 13C sidebands in the prior plan are about 1.307 and 2.076 MHz. The 1.968 us sampled window has FFT bin spacing 0.508 MHz and Nyquist 10.42 MHz; a densely sampled fit grid does not confer that frequency precision.

The old full-window raw and ratio screens peak at 1.187 and 1.192 MHz. The new raw and fitted-reference-line views peak at 0.882 MHz, whereas the point-wise ratio peaks at 1.623 MHz. At the predicted 1.692 MHz the new raw fitted amplitude is 1.225 kcps, but the full-window raw maximum is 1.533 kcps at 0.882 MHz; point-wise ratio gives 0.0250 at 1.692 MHz. The median new signal SEM across stored averages is 0.71 kcps per point; the raw amplitude is about 2.8% of the 44.27 kcps mean. The new signal rises from 40.46 to 46.92 kcps in its first eight points; excluding five points moves the raw peak to 0.781 MHz and ratio peak to 0.700 MHz, and excluding ten gives 0.998 and 1.057 MHz. This pronounced early-time shape and view/window dependence make the apparent 1.623 MHz ratio peak insufficient to establish det tracking. Ran `python ramsey_check.py`: raw and reference-aware comparisons, linear-baseline sinusoidal least squares frequency screens, detrended FFT, forward/reverse and early/late splits, reference changes in actual acquisition order, and exploratory exponential/Gaussian envelope fits. The 1.92 us span is only 1.92 nominal cycles; FFT bins are 0.508 MHz apart and the illustrative 0.385 MHz sideband spacing is below that scale. Frequency fitting between bins does not by itself resolve sidebands.

## Findings and interpretation

A structured early-time signal is visible in the raw signal readout: 40.70 kcps at 0.048 us, 45.92 at 0.528 us, 44.01 at 0.960 us and 47.20 at 1.344 us, while the reference remains around 48-49 kcps. Median across-average SEM is 1.14 kcps for signal and 1.12 kcps for reference; these pointwise values include between-average variation and do not establish independence across tau.

A linear-baseline sinusoid screens at 1.187 MHz and 1.68 kcps amplitude in raw signal; reference-line-normalized and pointwise-ratio screens peak at 1.187 and 1.192 MHz. The 1 MHz component is 1.28 kcps in raw signal; these are correlated projections over a short window, not distinct resolved peaks. Forward and reverse subsets both screen near 1.19 MHz (normalized amplitudes 0.037 and 0.032). A resampling sensitivity check under the same single-sinusoid model gives 1.168-1.204 MHz central 95% range; this excludes neither model bias nor drift. The previous 8 us review found a strongest ratio screen near 1.178 MHz, so the new feature is consistent with that prior observation and motivates a targeted detuning/sequence check, not a precise frequency or sideband assignment.

Reference averages vary substantially (42.02-55.19 kcps), with later count reduction; within-average first-to-last-quarter changes in acquisition order range from -4.2% to +6.7%. Forward/reverse agreement reduces concern about a simple direction-dependent artifact, but does not exclude drift, tracking changes, or baseline effects. Final counts fell from the preceding 44.184 to 35.122 kcps; no count-gate failure is reported. A TSP01/environment record is not supplied, so its contribution cannot be assessed.

Exploratory free-frequency envelope fits depend strongly on envelope model and baseline: an exponential fit gives about 3.05 us, whereas a Gaussian fit reaches the imposed 30 us upper bound with almost the same residual RMS (0.01665 versus 0.01689 normalized units). Neither is a defensible T2* measurement. The structure is compatible with a Ramsey-like response at early times; frequency offset, pulse/phase behavior, baseline drift, and other components remain plausible alternatives.

The earlier strong-pi pODMR supports selection of r03 as the aligned candidate under the project criterion. No well-supported numerical T2*, no very-short-T2* bound, no identified 13C coupling or absence of 13C, and no resolved 13C sidebands follow from these data. Next, use a targeted protocol diagnostic on r03, not another blind long Ramsey repeat: inspect the actual Ramsey timing/phase implementation and validate pulse/phase and readout contrast (e.g. calibrated Rabi/phase-cycled Ramsey); then design a detuning-shift comparison with matched short-tau sampling to test whether the ~1.19 MHz feature moves with programmed detuning. ## Files and context

- `measurement/m001.json` is the terminal raw export, including the saved sequence, per-average readouts, and scan order; `measurement/m002.json` through `m005.json` provide requested settings, result, status, and control. The run completed without an abort, with safe shutdown reported, 12 x 90,000 repetitions per tau and final counts 44.796 kcps; the terminal status shows no monitor error or stop request.

The prior state predates this completed measurement.
- Both scans used 41 points, tau=0.048 to 1.968 us in 0.048 us steps, mw=3.8759 GHz, and the same nominal shot budget and pulse settings; det changed from 1.0 to 1.5 MHz. The saved XML in m001 shows readout 1 is the zero-level reference and readout 2 the Ramsey signal for full_experiment=0. Prior ODMR supports r03 as the project's aligned candidate; this experiment does not independently establish alignment.

## Calculations and observations

`ramsey_analysis.py` reads the per-average arrays in tau order, checks scan-order drift, and compares raw signal, reference, signal/reference, and signal divided by a fitted reference line. It detrends with a linear baseline and screens a constant-amplitude sine and cosine at 0.5-3 MHz by least squares; amplitudes are sinusoidal half-amplitudes, and reported R2 gains are relative to the linear baseline. It also calculates detrended FFTs and subsets. A separate Python scratch calculation repeated the screen after excluding early delays. These are descriptive screens, not calibrated uncertainties or a physical decay fit.

- The 1.0 MHz run's ratio peak is 1.192 MHz (amplitude 0.0363, R2 gain 0.656); raw signal peaks at 1.188 MHz (1.683 kcps). The prior prediction for a +0.5 MHz det shift is about 1.692 MHz.
- In the new run the ratio screen peaks at 1.624 MHz (amplitude 0.0255, R2 gain 0.430); at 1.692 MHz it is 0.0251, R2 gain 0.411. This is compatible with a shifted component, but the apparent peak shift is 0.432 MHz and is not a precision measurement. The raw signal contains a 1.692 MHz component of 1.225 kcps (R2 gain 0.427), yet its strongest screen peak is 0.882 MHz (1.533 kcps, R2 gain 0.577); reference-line normalization also peaks at 0.882 MHz. The reference itself has a 0.924 MHz peak (0.405 kcps), so point-wise normalization materially changes the spectrum. Median across-average SEM of the new raw signal is 0.711 kcps per point, and the ratio SEM is 0.0126; these are point uncertainties, not significance estimates for a searched frequency.
- Excluding tau <=0.2 us moves the new ratio screen maximum to 0.746 MHz, although the 1.692 MHz fit still has amplitude 0.0190 and R2 gain 0.330. Forward/reverse ratio screens peak at 0.848/1.604 MHz, respectively, while first/last six averages peak at 1.594/1.660 MHz. Subsets have lower SNR and do not prove an artifact, but the sensitivity weakens carrier identification. The early signal rises from 40.46 to 46.92 kcps over the first eight points.
- Scan-order-aware common-mode linear brightness-drop scores, calculated using each stored snake order and the previous report's 15% threshold, flag no averages in either run; the new maximum is about 4.0%. This check does not exclude drift, tracking changes, or sequence artifacts. The 41-point FFT bin spacing is 0.508 MHz; zero-padding or a fine least-squares grid does not add resolving power. In particular, the expected 13C offset of about 0.385 MHz from the carrier is smaller than this bin spacing and the short observation window strongly mixes nearby components.

## Interpretation and limits

The ratio's shift from 1.192 to 1.624 MHz, and the raw component near 1.692 MHz, are suggestive of detuning-dependent Ramsey response. However, competing low-frequency structure in both raw channels, sensitivity to normalization and early points, and the short window prevent a clean identification. A transient, readout/baseline effects, drift, or sequence/timing artifacts remain plausible alternatives or contributors. The previous descriptive 6.33 us decay constant is not validated by this dataset. Neither a reliable T2* nor detection or absence of nearby 13C coupling is supported; these data do not resolve the expected carrier/sideband model or yield a robust envelope.

## Recommended next action

Audit the saved Ramsey sequence and active implementation/timing for how det changes phase and for tau-dependent readout or pulse artifacts, then design a targeted phase-cycling or matched control that distinguishes true det-following signal from the shared early transient and reference structure. Calculate predicted contrast and uncertainty for that control and choose a longer usable tau window only if coherence and SNR permit separating the approximately 0.385 MHz sideband offset. Recheck current tracking, drift, queue, and hardware/execute gates before any acquisition; this snapshot alone does not establish the live state. Do not run a blind repeat or report a T2* or 13C conclusion yet.

## Calculations and results

Ran `python ramsey_check.py` on both raw exports. It verifies that the 12 per-average arrays reproduce the combined data; uses readout 1 as reference and readout 2 as signal, consistent with the saved sequence and prior protocol review; checks raw signal, pointwise signal/reference, and signal divided by a fitted reference line; screens a linear baseline plus sinusoidal quadratures; and computes detrended FFTs and acquisition-order drift slopes. The frequency scans are exploratory, not statistical significance tests. The saved sequence calls the Ramsey function, while the earlier protocol review records its det-dependent second-pulse phase; the function itself is not in this snapshot.

Both short-tau datasets use 41 points from 0.048 to 1.968 us, 0.048 us spacing, 12 x 90,000 repetitions per point, and microwave frequency 3.8759 GHz. The new run changes det from 1.0 to 1.5 MHz. A simple phase-tracking model predicts that the earlier empirical 1.192 MHz feature would move to about 1.692 MHz; an unchanged feature would remain near 1.192 MHz. The existing field estimate gives a 13C Larmor frequency near 0.385 MHz: illustrative sidebands around the programmed 1.5 MHz are 1.115 and 1.885 MHz, or around the shifted empirical frequency 1.307 and 2.077 MHz. These are model targets, not proof that such sidebands must be visible.

The previous matched run has raw-signal and ratio screen maxima at 1.187 and 1.192 MHz. In the new run, the raw-signal maximum is 0.882 MHz (1.53 kcps sinusoidal amplitude); the fitted-reference-line view also peaks at 0.882 MHz, while the pointwise ratio peaks at 1.623 MHz (0.0255 amplitude). At the predicted 1.692 MHz the new raw amplitude is 1.225 kcps and ratio amplitude 0.0250; at the old 1.192 MHz they are 0.474 kcps and 0.0051. Removing the first four points (tau <= 0.192 us) moves the ratio maximum to 0.746 MHz and the raw maximum to 0.806 MHz. Forward and reverse subsets give ratio maxima at 0.848 and 1.604 MHz, respectively. These changes show that a det-following component is plausible in the ratio, but it is not the dominant or robust raw/readout-aware result.

The 1.92 us span gives nominal 1/span = 0.521 MHz, FFT bin spacing 0.508 MHz and Nyquist 10.42 MHz. Thus a 1 kHz screen grid does not imply 1 kHz resolving power; broad components, transient/baseline effects and nearby candidate frequencies are difficult to separate. The ratio FFT's largest bin in this range is 1.524 MHz with amplitude 0.0246. The actual snake-order common-mode linear end-to-start changes show no drop exceeding the previous review's 15% threshold (largest drop about 4%); this is an advisory drift screen, not proof of no drift.

The run is analyzable and contains structured signal, but the pointwise ratio's peak near the predicted shifted frequency depends on normalization and early points, while raw signal favors a lower frequency. No numerical T2* or nearby 13C coupling or absence is supported. # Ramsey review: r03, 2026-05-13

## Files and context

- `measurement/m001.json`: terminal savedexperiment raw export, including two readouts, four individual averages, effective variables and snake scan order. `measurement/m002.json` is the executed job; `m003.json` and `m004.json` report completion; `m005.json` is control. Final count was 38.249 kcps. The older running status in `evidence/e010.json` is superseded by terminal metadata.
- `project/state.md`, `project/advice.md`, `evidence/e003.json` and `evidence/e005.json` give the r03 selection, weak-pi 3.876 GHz grid minimum and protocol/model review. The inspected protocol in e005 says readout 1 is the mS=0 reference, readout 2 the Ramsey signal, and the second pi/2 phase advances with det*tau; the actual XML/function are not separately available in this snapshot.

## Checks and results

- Python (NumPy and SciPy) read the raw arrays, averaged the four traces, compared signal, signal/reference, and signal divided by a linear reference fit, computed mean-subtracted real FFTs, least-squares damped cosine fits, and linear common-mode slopes in acquisition order. No independent per-shot data were available. The measured scan is 0–6 us in 0.2 us steps, 31 points, 4 x 50,000 repetitions, programmed phase ramp 1.5 MHz. Stored data are in tau order; acquisition alternates forward/reverse.
- Signal alone has a broad oscillatory-looking component: raw mean at tau=0 is 38.10 kcps versus a fitted baseline about 42.1 kcps; the largest FFT bin is 0.968 MHz in raw signal, ratio and linear-reference-normalized views. The 31-point FFT bin spacing is 1/(31 x 0.2 us) = 0.161 MHz, with Nyquist 2.5 MHz; 1/6 us = 0.167 MHz is the approximate span-limited resolution. A bin is not a precise line or proof of a second spin. Mean across-point SEM estimated from the four signal averages is about 1.06 kcps, with only four samples; individual averages vary appreciably.
- Exploratory raw-signal fits `b + A exp[-(tau/T)^p] cos(2 pi f tau + phi)`, with f searched over 0–2.5 MHz, give for p=2: T=3.18 us, f=0.961 MHz, amplitude 2.30 kcps, residual SSE 33.98 versus 62.30 for a constant; p=1 gives T=2.06 us and f=0.962 MHz. Excluding tau=0 shifts T to 3.74 us (p=2) or 3.04 us (p=1); excluding the first five points makes the best fit favor about 0.24 MHz and reach the imposed 50 us T bound. These are unweighted descriptive fits with a frequency search, not confidence intervals or validated T2* estimates.
- Normalizing each channel by its own per-average mean and fitting the mean common mode against acquisition order gives end-minus-start slopes of +0.8%, -3.3%, -3.0%, +0.7% for averages 1–4. This simple linear check finds no large monotonic within-average drop; it does not exclude nonlinear drift, tracking changes, or fluorescence/phase noise. Mean reference levels range 43.68–46.59 kcps across averages. The earlier live estimate was 492.95 s per average, above the 450 s planning cap, although the pre-enqueue estimate was below it.
- Working field model from e005: B approximately 359 G and 13C Larmor approximately 0.385 MHz. Around the observed 0.96 MHz feature, a simple illustrative symmetric spacing would place features near 0.58 and 1.35 MHz, subject to the actual coupling and resonance model. FFT structure near those frequencies is not sufficient evidence of sidebands; the 1.5 MHz phase ramp is not itself proof of the observed carrier frequency, because detuning from the actual transition and aliasing can affect it. The weak-pi center was only established to the 1 MHz scan grid.

## Interpretation and limits

A Ramsey-like component near 0.96 MHz is plausible in the raw signal and both normalization views, with an apparent early decay. The fit is model- and window-sensitive and the frequency was selected from the same noisy data, so the signal and decay need replication before a quantitative coherence claim. Prior r03 strong- and weak-pi resonance evidence supports keeping this target; the completed measurement alone does not establish an accurate T2*, 13C coupling, a 13C-free environment, a resolved sideband, or the identity of any FFT feature. No statistical significance or detection limit for 13C has been established.

## Recommended next action

Re-track r03 and check a fresh weak-pi resonance if calibration age or drift warrants it, then repeat the Ramsey on the same 0–6 us, 0.2 us grid with more total shots and shorter per-average blocks, for example 8 x 25,000 as a starting design. This gives 200,000 shots per point, the same as the scout, but twice as many tracking opportunities; increase the even number of averages if the goal is improved shot-noise SNR (8 x 50,000 would nominally improve shot-noise SEM by sqrt(2), subject to drift and runtime). Recalculate the actual timing/advisory and recent drift before choosing repetitions: the 492.95 s live estimate exceeds the prior 450 s cap, and reducing repetitions alone may not suffice if fixed overhead dominates. Compare raw readouts and both normalization views, forward/reverse averages and an independently fitted oscillation/decay. If repeatable but the sideband question remains open, design a longer span and higher SNR only after a fresh timing and resolvability calculation; the present 6 us span gives only about 2.4 nominal resolution elements per 0.385 MHz spacing, before linewidth and noise are considered. No hardware job is submitted from this snapshot.

# Ramsey review: r03 short-tau diagnostic

## Files and context

- `measurement/m001.json` is the terminal savedexperiment raw export, including the saved sequence, two readouts, 12 per-average traces and snake scan order. `measurement/m002.json`-`m005.json` contain job, completion, status and stop metadata. The intended run completed without an abort or stop; final count text was 35.122 kcps. This is lower than the 42.367 kcps last noted at launch; it is not by itself proof of tracking loss.
- `project/state.md`, `project/advice.md`, `evidence/e003.json`, `evidence/e006.json` and `evidence/e017.md` provide the candidate selection, earlier Ramsey review and diagnostic model. r03 has a usable strong-pi resonance and fine weak-pi grid minimum at 3.8759 GHz. The earlier 8 us, det=1 MHz run had a weak 1 MHz component (0.277 kcps) and inconsistent per-average screens; the det=1.5 MHz scout was also inconclusive.
- Current run: tau 0.048-1.968 us, spacing 0.048 us, 41 points, det 1 MHz, microwave 3.8759 GHz, 12 x 90,000 repetitions per point. The saved XML places a polarized reference detection before the Ramsey block and the signal detection after it; the `ramsey` function implementation itself is not included in this snapshot.

## Calculations and observations

- `python ramsey_analysis.py` uses NumPy/SciPy to check the average against the stored traces, readout and reference-line normalization, acquisition-order common-mode trends, sinusoidal least squares, FFT, and exploratory damped-cosine fits. Times are in us, frequencies in MHz. The combined data equal the mean of the 12 traces to numerical precision.
- Raw signal rises from 40.70 kcps at 0.048 us to 46.39 at 0.672 us, falls to 44.75 at 1.008 us, rises to 47.20 at 1.344 us and falls to 43.50 at 1.968 us. The fitted reference line changes only 48.73 to 48.42 kcps; the shape remains in both pointwise and reference-line normalized data. Median empirical signal SEM across stored averages is 1.14 kcps per point and median pointwise-ratio SEM is 0.0127; averages include tracking and brightness changes, so these are descriptive, not independent shot-noise guarantees.
- A constant-baseline 1 MHz sinusoid has raw amplitude 1.22 kcps and reference-line-normalized amplitude 0.0251. The strongest nonzero unwindowed FFT bin is 0.508 MHz, with bin spacing 1/(41 x 0.048) = 0.508 MHz. A continuous sinusoid screen favors its 0.3 MHz lower search boundary for the combined data, indicating baseline/slow-shape ambiguity; zero padding would not add resolution. Odd/even snake-direction subsets yield different best screens (0.3 MHz boundary versus 1.27 MHz). They have only six averages each and are not conclusive independent replicates.
- Acquisition-order linear fits to the mean of the two readouts show a largest rise of 11.7% in average 7 and largest drop of 6.0% in average 10. The per-average reference mean ranges 42.02-55.19 kcps. This is a simple drift screen, not the project's full drift analyzer; signal shape can contaminate the common-mode slope. Snake directions are balanced, but drift and normalization remain relevant.
- As an explicit model check, fit baseline + A exp[-(tau/T)^p] cos(2 pi f tau + phase), without weights. At fixed f=1 MHz, raw fits give T=0.255 us (p=1) or 0.472 us (p=2), with RMS residuals 0.965 and 0.970 kcps; reference-line fits give 0.230 or 0.437 us. A free-frequency exponential fit instead gives raw T=1.00 us and f=1.216 MHz (RMS 0.876 kcps), and reference-line T=0.86 us and f=1.219 MHz. These are exploratory model-dependent fits, not T2* measurements; the frequency, envelope and baseline are not uniquely constrained.
- The prior model's expected 13C sidebands at approximately 0.615 and 1.385 MHz are 0.385 MHz from the programmed carrier. The 1.92 us endpoint span corresponds to a ~0.52 MHz inverse-span scale, too short to separate those components reliably. A peak or fitted component here cannot establish a sideband.

## Interpretation and unsupported claims

A real early-time signal structure is plausible: it is apparent in raw signal and both normalization views, and is much larger than the pointwise SEM at the earliest versus later points. It is compatible with Ramsey-like evolution, including possible rapid decay or beating, but the offset, slow trend, carrier mismatch, and snake-subset disagreement prevent a unique interpretation. The result does not establish a numeric T2*, prove that T2* is very short, or show a clean 1 MHz carrier. It neither demonstrates nor excludes nearby 13C coupling. The accepted r03 alignment remains based on the earlier pODMR evidence, not this Ramsey trace.

## Recommended next action

Keep r03 and investigate the signal/protocol before another blind repeat: inspect the actual `ramsey` waveform implementation and timing/phase convention, verify pulse calibration and readout roles, and compare current tracking/count and resonance with the recorded r03 settings. When live tools are available, perform the project's scan-order-aware drift analysis and check environmental provenance for the brightness change. Design a targeted phase or detuning-controlled diagnostic with a quantitative model and current drift/advisory limits; choose a tau span and SNR sufficient to distinguish the carrier and decay before fitting T2*. Only then design a longer, adequately resolved sideband measurement for 13C. The snapshot does not contain live hardware or the called waveform function, so those checks cannot be completed here.

# Ramsey review — r03 detuning-shift diagnostic

**Files used.** `project/brief.md`, `project/advice.md`, `project/state.md`, `context.json` and prior terminal review `evidence/e008.json` set the objective and comparison. `evidence/e006.json` is the preceding 1.0 MHz raw export; `evidence/e007.json` is its drift review. `measurement/m001.json` is the new terminal raw export, with job/settings and terminal status in `measurement/m002.json`–`m005.json`. Readout 1 is reference and readout 2 is Ramsey signal (`evidence/e008.json`). The project previously accepted r03 as aligned; this measurement does not independently establish alignment.

**Run and calculations.** The new 1.5 MHz detuning run completed without reported abort, with safe shutdown, 12 averages × 90,000 repetitions per point, and final count 44.796 kcps. The 41 points span 0.048–1.968 µs in 0.048 µs steps. `python ramsey_check.py` compares both raw exports: linear-baseline plus sine/cosine least-squares frequency screens, linearly detrended FFT, per-average SEM, resampling of averages, early-point exclusion and forward/reverse subsets. Additional Python calculations evaluated fixed-frequency fits and common-mode linear slopes in recorded acquisition order. The FFT bin spacing is 0.508 MHz, 1/span is 0.521 MHz, and Nyquist is 10.42 MHz; fitted frequencies are descriptive and the short-window spectral features overlap.

The previous ratio screen peaks at 1.192 MHz; a +0.5 MHz shift predicts 1.692 MHz. The new signal/reference ratio screen peaks at 1.623 MHz (amplitude 0.0255, linear-baseline residual reduction 43%); at 1.692 MHz it gives 0.0250 and 41%, while at 1.192 MHz it gives 0.0051 and 1.7%. Its strongest detrended FFT bin is 1.524 MHz. The new raw-signal screen also has a substantial 1.692 MHz component (1.225 kcps, 43% reduction), but its global maximum is 0.882 MHz (1.533 kcps, 58%). Dividing the signal by a fitted reference line retains the 0.882 MHz maximum, whereas pointwise reference normalization favors 1.623 MHz. Removing τ ≤ 0.2 µs moves the ratio maximum to 0.746 MHz; forward-only and reverse-only ratio maxima are 0.847 and 1.604 MHz. These are exploratory screens, not independent significance tests. Resampling the 12 averages gives a broad, multimodal frequency distribution (300 resamples, 2.5–97.5% about 0.814–1.679 MHz); it is not a validated confidence interval for a physical carrier.

The median across-average SEM is 0.711 kcps for signal and 0.0126 for per-average signal/reference ratios. In the recorded snake acquisition order, the largest linear common-mode brightness drop is 4.0% of the average brightness, below the prior review's 15% drop threshold; this simple check does not exclude other drift or readout artifacts. The previous run's formal scan-order review flagged no averages. New reference and signal means are 48.08 and 44.27 kcps; reference varies with τ, so pointwise normalization can affect the frequency screen.

**Interpretation.** A component near the predicted shifted frequency is present in both raw signal and ratio, consistent with detuning tracking; the fixed 1.192 MHz ratio component is weak in the new run. However, competing low-frequency structure, sensitivity to normalization, early points, and scan direction mean the comparison is suggestive rather than a clean confirmation of a coherent Ramsey carrier or proof that a fixed artifact has been excluded.

**Not supported.** Neither a reliable numeric T2* nor the presence, absence, or coupling strength of nearby 13C is established. The previous descriptive 6.33 µs fit is not a validated T2*: its 1.92 µs observation span is short and the model/readout dependence remains unresolved. Expected sidebands are not resolved well enough to attribute them to 13C; grid spacing in a frequency search is not physical spectral resolution.

**Recommended next action.** On the same accepted r03, first diagnose the early-time and reference-readout dependence using a targeted, sequence-validated control: repeat matched detunings with interleaved or balanced scan directions and a suitable phase/readout control, keeping per-average raw data. Predefine a joint analysis of raw signal, reference, ratio and fitted-reference normalization, including scan-order drift and uncertainties. If a reproducible detuning-tracking carrier survives those controls, extend the tau window with adequate sampling and signal-to-noise to measure decay and resolve candidate sidebands; only then fit T2* and assess 13C. This snapshot contains no live bridge access, so this is a recommendation, not an executed measurement.

- `measurement/m001.json`: terminal savedexperiment raw export, embedded `ramsey.xml`, scan order and all readouts/averages; `m002.json`-`m005.json`: job, terminal result, status and control. The saved sequence identifies readout 1 as polarized reference and readout 2 as post-Ramsey signal (`full_experiment=0`); the helper implementation of `ramsey` is not included in the snapshot.
- Ran `python ramsey_analysis.py` (NumPy/SciPy): checked [20 averages, 2 readouts, 41 points] against the stored mean; examined raw, signal/reference, signal/fitted-reference-line, fixed-frequency least squares with offset and linear baseline, FFT, first/last ten averages, and an acquisition-order residual-slope diagnostic. Separate local least-squares calculations compared early and late windows and standard errors of quadrature coefficients across averages. Those averages are tracking blocks, not fully independent experimental repeats. The available MATLAB drift analyzer was not run; our slope check is not its flagging algorithm.

## Findings and interpretation

- Accepted aligned candidate r03 remains the target. Fresh pODMR supported 3.8765 GHz on a 100 kHz grid, with several-100-kHz uncertainty. The new Ramsey used that center, det 1.5 MHz, tau 0.048-8.048 us at 0.2 us spacing; 1 million shots per point. The design's exponential-envelope model predicted a carrier near 1.5 MHz and illustrative 13C sidebands near 1.115 and 1.885 MHz for a 0.385 MHz nuclear frequency. Frequency offset and coupling can shift actual features. The 8 us span gives about 0.125 MHz nominal resolution and sampling has 2.5 MHz Nyquist; aliasing above Nyquist remains possible.
- Raw signal has a carrier-like component: full-span LS amplitude at 1.5 MHz is 0.705 kcps, versus median per-point signal SEM 0.850 kcps; fitting across points gives cosine/sine coefficients -0.616/0.344 kcps with across-average coefficient SEM 0.091/0.092 kcps. The raw, pointwise-ratio and fitted-reference-line screens all show a local peak near 1.515 MHz. First and last ten averages give 1.5 MHz amplitudes 0.668 and 0.766 kcps; this is useful within-run consistency, not independent replication. FFT bins near 1.46 and 1.59 MHz also carry power. Skip the first four points and the fixed 1.5 MHz amplitude remains 0.512 kcps. This supports a carrier-like contribution, but does not establish a clean single-frequency Ramsey decay.
- The strongest raw full-span screen is instead near 2.271 MHz, amplitude 0.818 kcps (0.555 after skipping four points); it also appears in both halves. Both features are stronger early: fixed-frequency amplitudes for points 0-19 versus 20-40 are 1.127 versus 0.313 kcps at 1.5 MHz and 1.400 versus 0.300 kcps at 2.27 MHz. The first signal point is 40.57 kcps versus a 44.83 kcps mean for points 10-40. A decaying coherent signal is plausible, but early-time transients, waveform/timing effects, leakage, aliasing, or multiple components remain alternatives. The strongest component is not accounted for by the original simple sideband model; the physical model needs testing rather than a forced fit.
- Fixed 1.115/1.885 MHz raw amplitudes are 0.146/0.261 kcps full span and 0.012/0.124 kcps after skipping four points. The reference itself has 0.232 kcps at 1.885 MHz, so the stronger ratio-side feature is particularly denominator-sensitive. There is no consistent resolved sideband pair. Median signal SEM is below the design's 1.21 kcps extrapolation, but observed 1.5 MHz amplitude is also below the prior 1.13 kcps short-tau screen.
- Reference and signal block means vary substantially (reference 41.74-54.90 kcps). Snake-order residual slopes after subtracting the overall tau trace show some within-block changes up to about 6.6 kcps across a sweep, not a validated drift-flag assessment. All 12 averages are present; combined data equal their mean. Median between-average per-point signal SEM is 1.14 kcps. - Raw signal rises from 40.70 kcps at 0.048 us to about 46 kcps around 0.5-0.7 us, dips near 0.9 us, rises near 1.3 us, then falls. Reference is comparatively flat across the combined tau scan; the ratio shows similar structure. First four points versus points 9-16 are lower in every average, by 0.73-6.55 kcps; direction-group mean differences are -4.69 and -3.93 kcps. This supports a reproducible early-time signal shape, though the per-average checks are not independent proof of a coherent carrier. Acquisition-order reference last-ten minus first-ten ranges -1.80 to +3.14 kcps, with both signs; tracking and between-average brightness changes remain relevant.
- A 1 MHz ideal carrier makes about 1.92 cycles over the 1.92 us span; the FFT bin spacing is 1/(41 x 0.048 us) = 0.508 MHz. The expected 13C sideband separation from the project model is about 0.385 MHz, smaller than that bin spacing. Fixed-frequency, linear-baseline sinusoid amplitudes in the raw signal are 1.10, 1.28 and 1.22 kcps at 0.615, 1.0 and 1.385 MHz, respectively; these highly correlated short-window screens cannot resolve distinct sidebands. Exploratory free-frequency raw fit with linear baseline and exponential envelope gives about 1.20 MHz and T = 2.98 us, but T's approximate covariance error is 2.07 us; a Gaussian-envelope fit hits the 10 us upper bound. Neither a numerical T2*, a robust upper or lower bound, nor the presence or absence of nearby 13C coupling is established. Do not assign the approximately 1.2 MHz feature to a specific nucleus or treat the fitted decay constant as a result.

These are exploratory, not uncertainty-qualified frequency estimates. The 1.920 us span corresponds to about 0.521 MHz inverse-span resolution; FFT bins are 0.508 MHz apart. The shifted ratio feature is compatible with the planned det-following hypothesis, but the raw-signal maximum, early-point sensitivity, and forward/reverse disagreement prevent a clean identification of it as a Ramsey carrier. A numerical T2*, a resolved 13C coupling or its absence, and a confirmed 0.5 MHz frequency shift are not supported. With 0.2 us sampling, Nyquist is 2.5 MHz; 31 samples give FFT bins spaced 1/(31*0.2 us) = 0.161 MHz (the 6 us endpoint span gives the approximate 0.167 MHz resolution scale). A 1.5 MHz phase ramp plus possible microwave resonance offset can plausibly yield an oscillation near 0.97 MHz; the prior weak-pi center is only grid-supported to about 0.5 MHz, and other shifts or artifacts are possible.

Oscillation and decay are plausible, but the data do not yet establish a reliable T2*.

## Unsupported claims and next action

Neither a precise T2*, a specific 13C coupling or nuclear-spin assignment, nor absence of 13C is supported. A single FFT peak does not establish the carrier or a sideband; the fitted frequency is not a direct new ODMR center measurement. Keep r03 as the target on the existing resonance evidence.

Median across-average SEM is 1.14 kcps for signal and 1.12 kcps for reference; individual averages have substantial common brightness changes (reference mean 42.0-55.2 kcps). First/second acquisition-half reference changes range roughly -1.27 to +2.10 kcps; these are descriptive drift checks, not a validated drift flag classification.

The raw signal's 1 MHz fitted amplitude is 1.28 kcps. The reference alone has only 0.21 kcps fitted at 1 MHz. Thus there is structured early-time signal, but its stability and frequency are uncertain, and per-point errors and correlated drift limit significance.

The nominal Fourier bin spacing is 1/(41 x 0.048 us) = 0.508 MHz; the model-plan 13C sidebands at 0.615 and 1.385 MHz are separated from the carrier by only 0.385 MHz. No quantitative T2*, resolved programmed carrier, nearby 13C coupling, or absence of 13C is established. - Ran `python ramsey_analysis.py` on both exports. It verifies stored-average means against combined data, estimates pointwise SEM across the 12 averages, computes a common-mode linear brightness slope in actual snake acquisition order (15% drop threshold), and screens a constant + linear baseline + sine/cosine at 0.4-3 MHz in raw signal, signal/reference, and signal/fitted reference line, both full grid and tau > 0.2 us. A separate Python detrended FFT check used the same exports. The per-average SEM is descriptive and can include drift and correlations.
- New run: raw means reference 48.08 and signal 44.27 kcps; median signal SEM 0.71 kcps and median per-average ratio SEM 0.0126. Early signal peak-to-peak through 0.75 us is 6.46 kcps. All 12 scan-order slope drops are below 15% (largest 4.0%); this check does not rule out other drift or artifacts. Earlier short-tau run had no drift flags, median signal SEM 1.14 kcps, and early peak-to-peak 5.69 kcps.
- The model in `evidence/e019.json` predicts that the prior 1.192 MHz feature shifts to approximately 1.692 MHz for a +0.5 MHz det change. Using the project's approximate 0.384 MHz 13C Larmor value, its corresponding illustrative sidebands are 1.307 and 2.076 MHz. These are model-dependent screening locations, not a complete hyperfine model.
- In the new full-grid screen the ratio peaks at 1.623 MHz (amplitude 0.0255), with amplitude 0.0250 at 1.692 MHz and 0.0240 at programmed 1.5 MHz. However raw signal and signal/reference-line peak at 0.882 MHz (raw amplitude 1.53 kcps); raw amplitude at 1.692 MHz is 1.23 kcps. Ratio amplitude at 1.192 MHz is only 0.0051. The earlier run's ratio and raw full-grid peaks were 1.192 and 1.187 MHz, amplitudes 0.0363 and 1.68 kcps respectively. Detrended FFT shows new signal bins at 1.016 and 1.524 MHz of similar amplitude (1.20 and 1.17 kcps), while ratio favors 1.524 MHz. The 1.920 us span gives nominal 1/span = 0.521 MHz and FFT bin spacing 0.508 MHz; oversampling the LS frequency grid does not improve physical resolution. Overlapping peaks, transient and baseline sensitivity prevent treating the best frequencies as precise measurements.

A real early-tau structure is visible in raw signal at a scale above the median point SEM. The ratio has a plausible det-shifted component near 1.6-1.7 MHz and the former 1.192 MHz component is weaker, which is compatible with a det-dependent contribution. But the raw low-frequency feature, normalization dependence, sensitivity to early points, and limited resolution leave the carrier interpretation ambiguous. A fixed artifact is not established either. The sequence phase mechanism and possible changes between sequential runs should be considered before attributing the shift to spin precession.

No reliable T2* value or decay bound, nearby 13C detection, coupling strength, or absence of 13C is supported. The earlier descriptive 6.33 us fit is not validated by a 1.92 us window. Nor do these data establish two resolved sidebands or a unique det-following carrier. The prior aligned-candidate conclusion remains the project context, not newly tested here.

Avoid another blind Ramsey repeat. On r03, inspect the active sequence and timing/readout calibration and design an alternate phase-cycled or otherwise controlled Ramsey measurement to discriminate coherent phase evolution from the shared early-time transient; include reference and control channels and explicitly model expected contrast and uncertainty. If a coherent carrier is established, choose a longer tau span and sampling/shot budget from that model to resolve decay and any candidate sidebands, with current drift and advisory limits checked before execution. The saved protocol basis in `e006.json` identifies readout 1 as reference and readout 2 as Ramsey signal and describes a second-pulse phase proportional to det x tau; the full external AWG function is not included in this snapshot.

## Calculations and observations

- Ran `python ramsey_analysis.py` (NumPy and SciPy): checked combined traces against the mean of all 12 saved averages, raw and fitted-reference-line signal, forward/reverse subsets, target-frequency linear least squares with a linear baseline, and exploratory exponentially and Gaussian-damped single-cosine fits. A second Python check screened raw and pointwise ratio frequencies after progressively excluding early points and compared first/last acquisition-order blocks per average.
- The combined raw signal rises from 40.70 kcps at 0.048 us to 46.39 kcps at 0.672 us, then has further structure; its range is 40.70-47.20 kcps. The reference has a fitted slope of -0.161 kcps/us and is much flatter over tau. Median pointwise signal SEM across the 12 averages is 1.14 kcps, but common-mode changes make those SEMs an imperfect measure of shape uncertainty. Reference means per average range from 42.02 to 55.19 kcps; some acquisition-order early/late changes occur, so drift is provenance. Forward and reverse subsets both show the broad structure and yield similar exploratory full-window peaks (~1.190 and ~1.185 MHz), reducing the likelihood that a simple unbalanced scan-direction artifact alone explains it. This block comparison is not the project's formal drift-flag analysis.
- Explicit model check: a simple 1 MHz phase oscillation has a 1 us period and is sampled at ~20.8 points per cycle. With a fitted linear baseline, full-window reference-line-normalized sinusoid amplitudes are 0.0264 at 1.0 MHz, 0.0227 at 0.615 MHz and 0.0251 at 1.385 MHz; the free-frequency screen peaks at 1.187 MHz. These are correlated, exploratory tests, not independent detections. Excluding data before 0.432 us shifts the raw best frequency to 1.027 MHz, showing sensitivity to the early transient and baseline. The 1.920 us span gives a nominal Fourier scale of ~0.52 MHz, wider than the ~0.385 MHz expected carrier-to-sideband separation; zero padding or a fitted peak cannot create the missing resolution.

There is reproducible early-time, readout-aware structure on r03, unlike the weak long-window carrier screen, consistent with a short-time Ramsey response or transient. No quantitative T2*, no 13C coupling or absence of 13C, and no resolved sidebands are supported. The strong-pi resonance supports the project's operational alignment selection, not a precise alignment angle. Stay on r03 and investigate the response before another blind Ramsey repeat: inspect the actual active Ramsey/AWG implementation and timing and verify pulse phase/detuning and readout behavior with a targeted calibrated control, such as a phase-cycled or quadrature short-tau test and a suitable reference/control, subject to the available sequence and safety/advisory checks. # Ramsey review — r03 det-shift diagnostic

## Files and context

- `project/state.md`, `project/brief.md`, and `project/advice.md`: objective, accepted r03 alignment and fine pODMR center 3.8759 GHz, and the predeclared det-shift test. Earlier Ramsey runs did not support T2* or 13C claims.

## Calculations and checks

Ran `python ramsey_check.py` on the two raw exports. It verifies that the mean of each stored average reproduces the combined raw readouts, uses readout 1 as reference and readout 2 as signal, fits a linear baseline plus sinusoid on a 0.25–2.25 MHz grid, checks raw signal, signal/reference and signal divided by a fitted reference line, screens subsets and halves, and calculates detrended FFT bins. It also computes common-mode linear drift in the recorded snake acquisition order. The new run's largest end-to-start drop is 4.0%, below the prior review's 15% flag threshold; this simple check is not a full hardware diagnosis. Median per-point SEM across averages is 0.711 kcps for signal and 0.0126 for the ratio.

The prior det=1.0 MHz ratio screen peaks at 1.192 MHz (amplitude 0.0363; raw signal peak 1.188 MHz). The new ratio peaks at 1.624 MHz (amplitude 0.0255), a +0.432 MHz shift versus the predicted +0.500 MHz; at the predeclared 1.692 MHz target its amplitude is 0.0250 and the sinusoid reduces linear-baseline residual sum of squares by 41%. The two new six-average halves peak at 1.594 and 1.660 MHz. The fixed 1.192 MHz component is much weaker in the new ratio (0.0051). These grid-screen values are descriptive, not independent resolved spectral lines or uncertainty estimates.

The evidence is mixed: new raw signal and fitted-reference-line screens instead peak at 0.882 MHz (1.53 kcps raw amplitude), and removing tau ≤0.2 µs moves the ratio peak to 0.746 MHz and the raw peak to 0.806 MHz. Individual averages have dispersed peaks. The new reference itself has a 0.924 MHz screen peak (0.405 kcps amplitude), so point-wise normalization and baseline structure matter. The 1.692 MHz target is present in raw signal (1.225 kcps amplitude), but is not its strongest component. FFT spacing is 0.508 MHz and 1/span is 0.521 MHz; zero padding or a finely sampled LS frequency grid does not create that resolving power. The expected 13C separation of about 0.385 MHz is below 1/span, and the expected 1.307 and 2.076 MHz target ratio amplitudes are 0.0095 and 0.0062, respectively.

## Interpretation and limits

The shift in the combined ratio is suggestive of a det-dependent contribution and weakens the simple fixed-1.192 MHz artifact explanation. It does not establish a clean physical carrier: the raw/readout-aware and transient-exclusion views favor a different component, the window is short, and other det-dependent artifacts or mixed components remain possible. The established r03 alignment/resonance conclusion remains the project basis.

A numerical T2*, a resolved 13C sideband/coupling, or absence of nearby 13C is not supported. In particular the earlier descriptive ~6.33 µs fit should not be promoted: the decay and signal model are not established over a ~1.92 µs span. The present result does not prove that T2* is very short or that the ratio peak is an artifact.

## Recommended next action

Perform a targeted protocol and readout investigation on r03 before another acquisition: inspect the Ramsey phase implementation and pulse calibration, reference behavior, and early-tau transient; design an alternate phase-cycled or quadrature control that can distinguish a det-following spin signal from readout/sequence artifacts. If that control establishes a reproducible carrier, plan a sufficiently long, adequately sampled tau window with SNR to resolve decay and the ~0.385 MHz splitting. Do not make a blind repeat or report T2*/13C from the current scans.

The script checks the mean against the four stored averages, compares raw readouts, signal/reference and signal divided by a linear fit to the reference, estimates common-mode slopes in actual acquisition order, computes mean-subtracted Hann-window FFTs, and fits illustrative damped cosines with exponential and Gaussian envelopes. The residual bootstrap is conditional on the selected exponential model and is not a complete uncertainty estimate.

- The signal shows a plausible short-lived oscillatory component, visible in the raw signal as well as both normalized views. A multistart raw exponential fit yields frequency 0.962 MHz, initial amplitude 3.19 kcps, envelope time 2.06 us, baseline 42.12 kcps, residual RMS 1.02 kcps and R2 0.48. A Gaussian envelope gives 3.18 us and R2 0.46; a point-wise-ratio exponential fit gives 2.39 us. The median signal SEM across four stored averages is 1.01 kcps per point; these averages are tracking intervals, not independent high-powered replications. Projections onto the fitted common waveform have the same cosine sign in all four, but amplitudes vary, and the waveform was selected from these same data.
- The exponential fit's conditional residual-bootstrap 2.5-97.5 percentiles are 0.79-8.21 us (400 resamples; 3 hit the 50 us upper bound). This ignores envelope choice, model selection, systematic errors and correlated drift. Thus the fit is a useful scout-scale estimate, not a well-supported T2* measurement.
- The raw and reference-line FFTs have a local peak at 0.968 MHz; the point-wise ratio also peaks there, but has other comparable features. At 0.2 us spacing the Nyquist frequency is 2.5 MHz; for 31 samples the FFT bins are 0.161 MHz apart (1/6 us = 0.167 MHz nominal span scale). A shifted resonance, phase convention, noise or other experimental effects are possible; the offset is not a direct field measurement.
- Using the project's approximate ms=+1 field model, (3.876-2.870) GHz / (2.8 MHz/G) = 359.3 G, giving a 13C Larmor scale of about 0.385 MHz. An illustrative on-resonance 1.5 MHz carrier would put symmetric features at 1.115 and 1.885 MHz, but this simple expectation is not a universal carbon signature and the carrier is uncertain. The final count is lower than the preceding weak-pi result's 43.890 kcps, but these are separate tracking/count observations. No temperature or humidity logs are supplied, so an environmental cause cannot be checked.

A Ramsey-like oscillation and an envelope on the order of a few microseconds are plausible working hypotheses. The low-amplitude late-time data, uncertain carrier and envelope dependence prevent a reliable numerical T2* claim. Neither 13C coupling nor its absence is established; no coupling strength, nuclear identification, precise resonance shift or improved alignment claim can be inferred from this scout alone. ## Calculations and interpretation

`python ramsey_analysis.py` uses NumPy/SciPy on the local raw export. The saved XML identifies readout 1 as the reference and readout 2 as the Ramsey signal. The array is 20 × 2 × 41; its average agrees with the exported combined data to 1.5e-14 kcps. The 0.2 µs step gives a 2.5 MHz Nyquist frequency; the 8 µs span gives roughly 0.125 MHz resolution (unwindowed 41-point DFT bin spacing 0.122 MHz). Stored snake order was used to calculate per-average normalized common-mode linear end-to-start changes: -6.5% to +13.8%, with no average falling below the project's -15% flag threshold. This check does not exclude other drift: average reference brightness ranges 41.7–54.9 kcps. Median empirical across-average SEM is 0.87 kcps reference and 0.85 kcps signal.

Constant-baseline FFT and sine/cosine screens of raw signal, signal/reference, and signal/fitted-reference-line all show a carrier-like 1.5 MHz component plus a stronger full-span feature near 2.27 MHz. Fitted-reference-line ratio amplitudes at 1.5 and 2.27 MHz are 0.0142 and 0.0169, respectively; after removing the first four points (tau < 0.848 µs), they are 0.0102 and 0.0114. At the prespecified 1.5 MHz, the paired two-coefficient Hotelling test after excluding four points gives T²=31.3, p≈0.00016 under independent averages; this does not rule out systematic pulse/readout artifacts. The 2.27 MHz feature was found by scanning frequencies, so a fixed-frequency significance calculation there is not a discovery p-value. It lies close to Nyquist and could reflect an aliased higher frequency or other structure.

The first signal point is 40.57 kcps versus 46.84 kcps at the second, with no corresponding large reference change. Exploratory single exponentially damped sinusoid fits are sensitive to the frequency band and first-point exclusion: the 1.2–1.8 MHz fit gives 0.22 µs at a frequency boundary with all points, but about 2.8–3.0 µs when the first one or four are removed; the 2.05–2.45 MHz fit gives about 1.65–2.99 µs across those windows. These are unweighted descriptive fits without a validated baseline or uncertainty model, not T2* estimates. A joint undamped two-frequency screen retains both components, so the second feature cannot be dismissed as simple leakage from a single fixed 1.5 MHz tone.

At the planned 1.115/1.885 MHz 13C targets, full-span reference-line amplitudes are 0.0026/0.0053; after the first four points they fall to 0.00036/0.00255. Refresh tracking and resonance as current evidence warrants; run the normal manifest, advisory, verifier and safety checks before any hardware job. It checks the combined trace against the mean of four stored averages, raw readouts, pointwise pooled signal/reference, acquisition-order linear common-mode brightness slopes, FFTs of raw/normalized and individual/direction-group traces, and exploratory single-frequency exponential and Gaussian envelope fits. The FFT uses 31 samples, so its actual bin spacing is 1/(31 × 0.2 us) = 0.161 MHz and Nyquist is 2.5 MHz; 1/6 us = 0.167 MHz is the approximate inverse-span scale. The 0.968 MHz feature is strongest in the forward pair; the reverse pair has its largest peak at 0.806 MHz. ## Files and provenance

- New terminal raw export: `measurement/m001.json`; job/settings and terminal status: `measurement/m002.json` through `m005.json`. The 1.5 MHz run completed 12 x 90,000 repetitions per tau, 41 points from 0.048 to 1.968 us, step 0.048 us, at 3.8759 GHz. The bridge reports no abort, successful safe shutdown, no stop request or monitor error, and final counts 44.796 kcps.
- Comparison: prior 1.0 MHz short-tau terminal raw export `evidence/e006.json`, drift and prior review `e007.json` and `e008.json`, and det-shift model/design `e019.json`. The two runs have the same tau grid and shot budget. `project/state.md`, `project/advice.md`, `md/memory.md`, and `context.json` provide project history and readout/interpretation context. The saved sequence in each raw export specifies reference readout 1 and Ramsey signal readout 2 for `full_experiment=0`; the phase implementation is reported by `e019.json`, not independently present as the Ramsey function in this snapshot.
- Prior project review accepted r03 from strong-pi pODMR, with refined weak-pi grid center 3.8759 GHz; this review does not independently re-evaluate those resonance datasets. Earlier long-tau Ramsey measurements were also inconclusive.

## Calculations and checks

- Run `python ramsey_analysis.py` from this directory. The script compares raw signal, signal/reference, and signal divided by a linear fit to the reference. It fits a linear baseline plus sine and cosine over 0.35-3.0 MHz, screens detrended FFTs, checks per-average scan-order drift, compares direction groups, and bootstraps stored averages. `ramsey_comparison.png` plots the two raw and ratio traces. Frequency-screen amplitudes are sinusoidal amplitudes, not peak-to-peak values; the reported R2 improvements are relative to a linear baseline.
- The new early (tau <= 0.75 us) signal spans 6.46 kcps and the ratio 0.134; median across-average SEM is 0.71 kcps for signal and 0.0126 for per-average ratios. The previous run spans 5.69 kcps and 0.111, with respective SEM 1.14 kcps and 0.0127. These SEMs describe variation of stored averages, not a complete systematic uncertainty. New reference averages 48.08 kcps, signal 44.27 kcps; the reference itself has a spectral minimum-residual feature near 0.924 MHz.
- The prior 1.0 MHz run's ratio screen peaks at 1.192 MHz (amplitude 0.0363, baseline-relative R2 improvement 0.656); raw peaks at 1.187 MHz (1.68 kcps, 0.681). If that feature is a single det-following carrier with the assumed sign, increasing det by 0.5 MHz predicts 1.692 MHz. In the new run the ratio screen peaks at 1.623 MHz (0.0255, 0.430); at 1.692 MHz it gives 0.0250 and 0.411. Raw signal instead peaks at 0.882 MHz (1.53 kcps, 0.577), with a secondary local minimum in residual error near 1.629 MHz; at 1.692 MHz it gives 1.22 kcps and 0.427. The fitted-reference-line view also peaks at 0.882 MHz. Removing tau <= 0.2 us moves the new ratio peak to 0.746 MHz and the raw peak to 0.806 MHz. These are exploratory single-sinusoid fits, not resolved component estimates.
- The 1.92 us delay span has nominal 1/span = 0.521 MHz resolution; the unpadded FFT bin spacing is 0.508 MHz, and Nyquist is 10.42 MHz. Closely spaced carrier and 13C sideband hypotheses are therefore not independently resolved by this scan. The 0.001 MHz LS grid is interpolation, not frequency resolution. For the project's illustrative 13C frequency 0.385 MHz, sidebands around 1.692 MHz would be near 1.307 and 2.077 MHz; this is a model target, not evidence of coupling.
- Snake-order brightness-slope check, using the saved acquisition order and the prior review's 15% drop threshold, flags no new averages (largest drop score 0.040). This does not exclude scan-order or other systematic effects: the six forward averages give new raw/ratio screen peaks 0.862/0.847 MHz, while the six reverse averages give 1.614/1.604 MHz. Each subset has half the data and individual averages are noisy, so the difference warrants a control, not a definitive drift diagnosis. An exploratory 400-resample bootstrap of independently resampled averages gives ratio-screen shift 2.5/50/97.5 percentiles -0.390/0.380/0.505 MHz, with 55% in +0.3 to +0.7 MHz; this is model- and resampling-dependent, not a calibrated confidence interval for a physical frequency.

## Interpretation and limits

The new trace contains a substantial early-time variation in raw signal. A component near the predicted shifted carrier appears in both raw and normalized data, and the normalized peak is compatible with tracking, but the stronger raw low-frequency feature, sensitivity to normalization and early-point exclusion, and direction split prevent a clean identification. The reference has structure in the same low-frequency region, making common-mode brightness or a protocol/scan-order artifact plausible; a physical Ramsey contribution is also plausible. A joint single-sinusoid screen favors a +0.5 MHz shift over a fixed frequency, but it cannot settle the assignment when the preferred raw and ratio components differ.

No reliable T2* value, nearby-13C coupling or absence, or uniquely established det-following carrier follows from these data. In particular, the earlier descriptive 6.33 us fit is not a supported T2*. Completion and a negative slope-based drift flag do not establish absence of systematic error.

## Recommended next action

Before another long acquisition, inspect the actual active `ramsey` pulse/phase implementation and calibrate pulse contrast and phase on r03, then design an interleaved, phase-cycled or otherwise validated control that compares at least two detunings and balances or randomizes tau order. Specifically test whether the 0.88 and 1.6-1.7 MHz features follow phase/detuning and persist independently of reference and acquisition direction. Use current tracking, drift and advisory limits before any hardware run; the snapshot contains no live bridge state.

For a subsequent 13C/T2* measurement, model expected contrast and decay against measured noise before choosing the range and shot budget. An illustrative 0-8 us grid with 0.1 us spacing has 1/span = 0.125 MHz and 5 MHz Nyquist, potentially resolving a 0.385 MHz separation if coherence and SNR survive; earlier 8 us data were weak, so resolution alone does not guarantee detectability. For example, a hypothetical 1.7 kcps initial amplitude would fall at 4 us to 0.031 kcps for exponential T2* = 1 us or 0.90 kcps for T2* = 6.33 us, versus the present 0.71-1.14 kcps median per-point SEM range. These are planning scenarios, not measured T2* values; use a validated signal and actual noise to select the final design.

# Ramsey review: image145844 re-image r03

## Data and context

Historical Ramsey comparisons below are from the project state, not a reanalysis of their raw data.

The new Ramsey completed 20 x 50,000 shots per point, with per-average tracking, final counts 43.433 kcps, no abort or reported monitor error. It scanned 0.048-8.048 us in 41 points, at 3.8765 GHz and programmed detuning 1.5 MHz. Snake acquisition order is recorded and data are saved in tau order. The embedded active sequence shows readout 1 is the zero-level reference and readout 2 is the Ramsey signal; the optional one-level reference is skipped (`full_experiment=0`).

## Calculations and observations

- Ran `python ramsey_analysis.py`, `python ramsey_checks.py`, and `python ramsey_pair_check.py`; `ramsey_review.png` shows the raw and normalized traces and split averages. Least-squares frequency screens include a constant and linear baseline plus sine and cosine; a joint two-frequency screen and an average-resampling bootstrap are exploratory. The scan step gives a 2.5 MHz Nyquist frequency, and the 8 us span gives about 0.125 MHz nominal frequency resolution.
- The mean signal/reference is 44.67/48.79 kcps; median across-average per-point SEM is 0.85/0.87 kcps respectively. Raw signal, signal/reference and signal divided by a fitted reference line all show coherent structure. The raw single-frequency screens peak near 1.515 MHz (amplitude 0.72 kcps) and 2.271 MHz (0.82 kcps). They persist in the first versus last 10 averages and forward versus reverse scans, and after excluding the first 4 points; per-average frequency screens are noisy and inconsistent. Reference-channel peaks differ, so these are not simply reproduced reference fluctuations. The fixed, preplanned 1.5 MHz raw component has amplitude 0.705 kcps; an across-average coefficient test gives p about 3e-7 under its independence/model assumptions, not a search-corrected significance for the selected peaks.
- A joint undamped two-sinusoid raw fit gives 1.523 and 2.265 MHz, midpoint 1.894 MHz and half-separation 0.371 MHz. Excluding the first 10 points gives 1.511 and 2.277 MHz, half-separation 0.383 MHz. The 1,000-resample across-average bootstrap for the full-span stationary two-tone model gives half-separation 0.360-0.382 MHz (central 95% interval); this is conditional on that selected model, not a total uncertainty for a decaying or drifting signal.
- Under the project working model, B = (3.8765 - 2.8700) GHz / (2.8 MHz/G) = 359.5 G and the 13C Larmor frequency is about 0.385 MHz. The half-separation is of that order, though the full-span conditional interval falls slightly below 0.385 MHz. A symmetric sideband interpretation would put the carrier near 1.894 MHz, about +0.394 MHz from the programmed 1.5 MHz; this is comparable to, but at the high end of, the stated several-hundred-kHz pODMR uncertainty and requires an effective detuning offset. The nominal 1.885 MHz high-sideband target is weak in raw signal and does not survive the skip-4 check. The high-frequency peak is close enough to Nyquist that aliasing is a real ambiguity.
- A descriptive raw two-frequency fit with a shared exponential envelope gives 3.06 us for the full span but 1.84 us after removing the first 10 points; a single damped sinusoid prefers the other peak and gives about 1.80 us. These are competing empirical models, not validated T2* measurements. Stored average mean references vary from 41.74 to 54.90 kcps. A simple acquisition-order common-mode slope check reaches about 13% across average 3; this is not the project's formal drift-flag analysis, which is unavailable for this new run.

## Interpretation and limits

The run provides substantially stronger raw/readout-aware evidence of coherent oscillatory structure than the earlier non-claim-grade Ramsey scans. A pair of carbon-related sidebands around an offset carrier is a plausible, testable explanation; independent tones, pulse/sequence artifacts, aliasing, drift and model-dependent spectral leakage remain alternatives. The prior short det-shift diagnostic showed movement away from a fixed 1.192 MHz feature, but its short span and mixed screens do not establish that these new peaks track detuning.

A numerical T2*, a 13C assignment/coupling strength, and a negative conclusion that no nearby 13C exists are not yet supported. The presence of a 1.5 MHz component alone does not establish it as the carrier; the pair spacing alone does not uniquely identify 13C. Do not treat conditional bootstrap precision as a physical uncertainty or infer sub-grid precision for the pODMR center.

## Recommended next action

On the same r03, first check current tracking/counts and refresh the resonance if needed; inspect the active sequence and satisfy the live bridge, queue, verifier and runtime limits. Design a detuning-shift control at 1.2 MHz, paired or interleaved with a 1.5 MHz reference while retaining the same microwave frequency and suitable 8 us sampling. If both positive-frequency components are physical sidebands that track the programmed detuning and the resonance remains stable, the pair should move approximately from 1.52/2.27 to 1.22/1.97 MHz, retaining its separation; allow for any independently measured resonance change and test for aliasing. Compare raw, reference-line and point-wise traces, acquisition directions and uncertainty; use a validated multi-component decay model only if the control supports the signal interpretation. Model visibility and verify current hardware conditions before any submission. If the control fails, investigate pulse/sequence and alias artifacts rather than blindly repeating the same Ramsey scan.

# Ramsey review: r03 short-tau diagnostic

## Files and data

- `measurement/m001.json`: terminal raw savedexperiment export, including the embedded sequence, both readouts, 12 stored averages, and snake scan order. `measurement/m002.json`-`m005.json`: job, completed result, status and control. The run completed without abort or reported monitor error; final count text was 35.122 kcps (above the 20 kcps run gate), down from 44.184 kcps in the preceding run. The snapshot does not contain TSP01 logs to explain that difference.
- `project/state.md`, `project/advice.md`, `md/memory.md`, and `md/knowledge.md`: objective, alignment and earlier measurements. `evidence/e001.json`-`e003.json` and `evidence/e006.json`/`e017.md`: previous 8 us Ramsey data/review and this diagnostic's model and design. The project accepts r03 from strong-pi ODMR and uses the fine weak-pi grid center 3.8759 GHz; the two previous Ramsey runs did not support T2* or 13C claims.
- New run: `auto__ramsey`, 41 tau points, 0.048-1.968 us in 0.048 us steps, programmed detuning 1.0 MHz, 12 x 90,000 repetitions per point. Embedded sequence with `full_experiment=0` identifies readout 1 as the mS=0 reference and readout 2 as Ramsey signal. The prior protocol review `evidence/e003.json` records that det advances the second pulse phase; the AWG function itself is not in this snapshot.

## Calculations and checks

- Ran `python ramsey_analysis.py` on the terminal export; it verifies finite data and that the 12-average mean reproduces the saved combined traces, evaluates linear acquisition-order common-mode drift separately for each snake-ordered average, screens sinusoidal least-squares components with a linear baseline, compares forward/reverse and temporal subsets, explores damped-cosine fits and paired-average bootstrap, and creates `ramsey_review_plot.png`. Also calculated FFT bins and paired early-minus-middle contrasts separately with Python. Average-to-average SEM is descriptive and points share common-mode variations.
- Raw signal rises from its first four points (0.048-0.192 us) to points 10-13 (0.480-0.624 us): paired difference early minus middle = -4.38 kcps, SEM 0.57 kcps, approximate 95% t interval [-5.64, -3.12] kcps across 12 averages. Reference difference is +0.10 +/- 0.47 kcps SEM; pointwise signal/reference difference is -0.092 +/- 0.009 SEM. All 12 signal differences have the same sign; both scan directions show the feature. The selected windows are descriptive, and stored averages are tracking blocks, not fully independent replicated experiments.
- Mean reference and signal are 48.57 and 44.65 kcps; median pointwise across-average SEM is 1.12 and 1.14 kcps, respectively. Acquisition-order normalized common-mode linear end-to-start changes range from -6.2% to +11.8%, with none crossing the prior -15% drift flag threshold. This simplified check does not exclude nonlinear drift or changes between averages.
- A linear-baseline, undamped sinusoid screen gives signal amplitudes 1.28 kcps at 1.0 MHz, 1.10 at 0.615 MHz and 1.22 at 1.385 MHz; the strongest scanned component is 1.187 MHz (1.68 kcps). The reference-line-normalized trace gives the same broad pattern. Forward and reverse subsets peak near 1.19 MHz, but the last six averages have their maximum at the 0.5 MHz lower boundary of the restricted screen. The FFT spacing is 1/(41 x 0.048 us) = 0.508 MHz; the expected carrier-to-sideband separation of about 0.385 MHz is smaller, so these overlapping screens do not resolve sidebands. The prior 8 us run's 1 MHz component was only 0.277 kcps, with its largest screen near 1.178 MHz.
- The project model is S(t) = baseline + A exp(-t/T2*) cos(2 pi f t + phase). Exploratory raw-signal fits show severe model dependence: with a linear baseline and f fixed at 1.0 MHz, T2* is 0.186 us; allowing f to vary yields f = 1.196 MHz and T2* = 2.98 us, with a different baseline and lower residual. These are descriptive fits, not measurements or confidence bounds; the fixed-frequency curve also misses later structure. A 2 kcps initial amplitude with T2* = 0.25 us was projected to give only about 1.9 kcps early peak-to-peak against the planned 1.17 kcps per-point SEM, so a weak or very fast component is not ruled out.

## Interpretation and limits

The new run establishes a substantial early tau-dependent readout feature, stronger and more reproducible than the previous long-window carrier screen. An oscillatory Ramsey contribution is plausible, but the early rise plus later structure can also reflect a baseline/transient or a more complicated response. The broad ~1.19 MHz screen is not a precision frequency measurement, and its relation to the 1 MHz programmed phase evolution remains unverified. Frequency, phase, envelope, baseline, and drift are confounded over this short window.

A numeric T2*, an upper or lower bound on T2*, a resolved 13C sideband or coupling, and the absence of nearby 13C are not supported. The strong early response alone neither establishes very short T2* nor explains the earlier weak long-window response. The original alignment conclusion remains based on the prior ODMR evidence, not this Ramsey feature.

## Recommended next action

On r03, first check current tracking/counts and calibrate the actual Ramsey pi/2 pulse and readout/phase behavior using a targeted Rabi or pulse-phase control. Then design a balanced, interleaved short-tau detuning/phase diagnostic at 1.0 and 1.5 MHz: a genuine phase-driven component should shift by approximately 0.5 MHz in signed frequency, subject to the sequence's sign convention and any physical detuning; a stationary transient need not. The present ~0.508 MHz Fourier-bin spacing makes this comparison marginal, so model the expected waveforms and noise first and extend the useful time span or use phase-sensitive fitting if resolvable; reassess drift and the active per-average advisory cap before execution. If a robust carrier and envelope emerge, acquire a suitably longer, higher-resolution scan for T2* and 13C; otherwise use an alternate protocol rather than a blind repeat. No hardware action was performed in this review.

Confirmed 12 × 2 × 41 per-average arrays reconstruct the combined raw readouts, and used saved snake acquisition order. Linear-baseline plus sine/cosine least-squares screens from 0.25–2.25 MHz were applied to raw signal, signal/reference and signal divided by a fitted reference line, with full and tau > 0.2 µs views. Screen maxima and amplitudes are descriptive, not fitted uncertainties or independent spectral lines.

For det = 1.5 MHz, ratio peak is 1.624 MHz, amplitude 0.0255, versus predicted 1.692 MHz; at 1.692 MHz amplitude is 0.0251 and the sinusoid reduces linear-baseline residual sum of squares by 41%. Raw signal and fitted-reference-line views instead peak at 0.882 MHz; raw amplitude is 1.53 kcps there and 1.22 kcps at 1.692 MHz. The forward and reverse six-average ratio screens peak at 0.847 and 1.604 MHz respectively; individual maxima vary. Direction is confounded with average number and shot noise, so this is a reproducibility concern, not proof of scan-order drift. A component near the predicted 1.692 MHz and a reduced 1.192 MHz component are consistent with detuning response, but the competing ~0.88 MHz raw feature, reference structure, and unstable peak selection prevent a clean carrier identification. Do not claim detection or exclusion of nearby 13C: the planned ~1.307/2.076 MHz sideband positions have no independently resolved, repeatable carrier-plus-sideband pattern. Before another acquisition, inspect the actual Ramsey pulse/detection and det-phase implementation and reference channel behavior, then design a controlled, interleaved det = 1.0/1.5 MHz comparison on r03 with balanced or randomized tau order, stable tracking/readout checks, and a phase-cycled or no-microwave reference control if the validated protocol supports it.
